analysis.one_liner: Raises car fuel economy standards, cuts home energy bills, and repeals oil, gas, coal, and nuclear tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of its four committees and expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised fuel economy requirements for cars and SUVs to 40 miles per gallon, removed the cap on tax credits for hybrid buyers, created manufacturing credits for efficient vehicles, and doubled funding for home weatherization. It would have required electric and gas utilities to cut customer energy use and to buy a rising share of renewable power, and let homeowners who generate their own solar or wind power credit it against their bills. It also repealed a set of subsidies, royalty relief, and tax breaks that the 2005 energy law had given to oil, gas, coal, and nuclear companies, and restored states' authority to set their own efficiency and fuel economy rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers save on gasoline as fuel economy standards rise and tire efficiency rules take effect; low-income households get warmer, cheaper homes through doubled weatherization funding; utility customers benefit from mandated efficiency savings; homeowners with rooftop solar or wind gain guaranteed net metering; and taxpayers save as oil, gas, coal, and nuclear subsidies are repealed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, utility customers, and low-income homeowners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the passenger car fuel economy standard in steps from 25 mpg to 40 mpg by model year 2017, and raises civil penalties for violations from $5 to $10 per vehicle with inflation indexing [S3].
Doubles authorized weatherization assistance funding, which pays to insulate and weatherproof low-income homes, cutting heating and cooling bills [S3].
Repeals the cap on the number of hybrid and advanced-technology vehicles eligible for the consumer tax credit, so more buyers qualify [S3].

Requires retail electricity and natural gas suppliers to achieve rising annual energy savings (up to 3.75%) and electric suppliers to meet a federal renewable portfolio standard reaching 20% by 2030, with a net metering standard so customers with small solar, wind, or fuel cell installations get credited for power they feed back to the grid [S3].

Repeals Energy Policy Act of 2005 provisions giving oil and gas royalty relief, deep-water and Alaska offshore royalty suspension, and tax credits for advanced nuclear, clean coal, coke, and refining facilities [S3].
Closes the tax loophole that let heavy SUVs be written off as business equipment, subjecting them to the luxury auto depreciation limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose royalty relief and production incentives; coal, nuclear, and refining companies lose tax credits; automakers face higher fuel economy mandates, higher penalties, the end of the SUV depreciation break, and the end of federal preemption of state fuel economy rules; electric and gas utilities must fund efficiency programs and buy renewable power; the tax credits for efficient vehicles and renewables are paid for with federal revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, coal, nuclear, automakers, utilities

drawbacks.text: The bill layers new costs on industry: a federal renewable mandate and efficiency resource standard raise compliance costs that utilities can pass to ratepayers, and the 40 mpg mandate plus higher civil penalties increase vehicle production costs that show up in car prices [S3].

Repealing federal transmission siting authority and FERC permit coordination could slow new long-distance power lines and gas storage needed for grid reliability, a concern supporters of the 2005 energy law raised [S3].

The new manufacturing credits allocate up to $1 billion per year in tax credits to vehicle makers, and extended renewable credits reduce federal revenue, so some of the consumer benefit is financed by taxpayers rather than by the industries alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer savings are real and broad — lower gasoline and utility bills, warmer low-income homes, taxpayer money no longer flowing to mature energy industries — while the main costs (higher car prices, possible rate impacts, forgone revenue from credits) are real but smaller and partly transitional. The bill's design is conventional for energy policy: it pairs standards and mandates with tax credits, and it deliberately shifts support from fossil and nuclear toward efficiency and renewables. Its main flaw is breadth; repealing federal transmission siting authority could complicate grid expansion even as the renewable mandate increases the need for it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees and two subcommittees without ever getting a markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT), with Rep. Maurice Hinchey, introduced the bill on November 17, 2005 [S1].

The Speaker referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' [S5].
Within a month it was sent to two subcommittees, Highways, Transit and Pipelines and Energy and Air Quality, where it stayed [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, killing it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, coal, and nuclear companies kept the royalty relief and tax subsidies the bill would have repealed; automakers kept the SUV depreciation break and lower fuel economy standards; utilities avoided the efficiency and renewable mandates. Ordinary taxpayers and energy consumers, who would have paid for those subsidies in taxes and fuel, did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, coal, nuclear, and auto interests

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with 27 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsoring — but with no recorded votes or floor debate, the record shows only that the Republican-majority committees never acted, not how the chamber would have divided.

industries.note: The bill repeals Energy Policy Act of 2005 royalty relief, in-kind royalties, deep-water and Alaska offshore royalty suspensions, and related tax incentives — subsidies paid for by taxpayers and forgone federal royalties. Its interests ran against the bill's public-benefit provisions.
The bill repeals tax credits for advanced nuclear facilities, clean coal investment, coke production, refinery expensing, and related depreciation benefits enacted in the 2005 energy law.

Automakers face phased fuel economy mandates rising to 40 mpg, doubled civil penalties, an end to the SUV depreciation loophole, and loss of federal preemption of state fuel economy rules — but gain a new tax credit program of up to $1 billion per year for building efficient vehicles and components. Consumers get fuel savings; buyers pay for the efficiency in vehicle prices.

Utilities must meet a federal efficiency resource standard and a renewable portfolio standard reaching 20% by 2030, with fees or penalties for falling short, and must offer net metering to customers with rooftop solar and wind. Compliance costs can flow to ratepayers, but the mandates also cut the fuel and generation costs behind utility bills.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency industries
industries.note: Extended renewable production and residential credits, a federal renewable mandate with tradeable credits, net metering, doubled weatherization funding, and Energy Star funding all expand demand for wind, solar, insulation, and efficiency services — and cut ordinary households' bills at the same time.
The bill creates a national tire fuel efficiency program with minimum efficiency standards and mandatory retailer labeling, adding compliance costs for tire makers while saving drivers fuel.
